topics.name: California gold rush
topics.kicker: Gold found at Sutter’s Mill in 1848 · Brought the forty-niners west
topics.briefing: In January 1848, a carpenter named James Marshall spotted shiny flakes in the water channel of a sawmill in the Sierra Nevada foothills. Within a year, word had spread around the world, and an estimated 300,000 people eventually rushed to California, most of them men who became known as “forty-niners.” A few struck it rich, more made money selling them supplies, and California’s Native peoples suffered terrible losses.
topics.answerHtml: California gold rush (accept Gold Rush of 1849; prompt on gold rush; do not accept “California” alone or “Klondike Gold Rush”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1850, California’s legislature passed a Foreign Miners’ Tax that charged non-citizens $20 a month, driving away many Mexican and other Latin American miners during this event. A later version of the tax fell mostly on Chinese immigrants, who called California “Gold Mountain.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event that began after James Marshall found gold at Sutter’s Mill in 1848.

tossups.p: People who took part in this event described the hardships of the journey, and the letdown of finding little, as “seeing the elephant.” Many of them reached the Pacific coast by sailing around Cape Horn or by crossing the Isthmus of Panama.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event that drew the “forty-niners” west after gold was found at Sutter’s Mill.

tossups.p: Participants in this event were nicknamed “Argonauts,” after the Greek heroes who sailed with Jason in search of the Golden Fleece. Many of them sang new words to Stephen Foster’s song “Oh! Susanna” as they headed west.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event that drew tens of thousands of “forty-niners” west after 1848.

tossups.p: This event began when a carpenter noticed shiny flakes in the tailrace of a sawmill on the South Fork of the American River. Nine days later, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed by negotiators who had no idea that the discovery had been made.
tossups.r: That carpenter was James Marshall. For 10 points, name this event that began at Sutter’s Mill in January 1848.

tossups.p: The merchant Sam Brannan helped set off this event by running through the streets of San Francisco waving a bottle of gold dust, after stocking his store with picks and pans. Brannan grew rich by selling supplies to the people who joined this event.
tossups.r: It began after James Marshall found gold at Sutter’s Mill. For 10 points, name this event that brought the “forty-niners” to California.

tossups.p: President James K. Polk set off a frenzy in December 1848 when he confirmed the discovery that started this event in his annual message to Congress. Soon, tens of thousands of fortune seekers were heading west by land and by sea.
tossups.r: They were called “forty-niners.” For 10 points, name this event that began when gold was found at Sutter’s Mill.

tossups.p: During this event, a Bavarian-born merchant named Levi Strauss opened a dry-goods business in San Francisco. In 1873, he and the tailor Jacob Davis patented denim work pants that were strengthened with copper rivets.
tossups.r: Those pants became blue jeans. For 10 points, name this event that brought thousands of miners to California after 1848.

tossups.p: In 2019, California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, formally apologized to Native Californians for the state’s violence against them during and after this event, calling it a genocide. An 1850 state law let settlers force Native people, including children, into unpaid labor, and the Native population fell from an estimated 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event that began when James Marshall found gold at Sutter’s Mill in 1848.

tossups.p: After this event began, the Land Act of 1851 forced Californios, Spanish-speaking landowners of Mexican descent, to prove their land titles in American courts, and many lost their ranches. Delegates at Monterey had already written a state constitution that banned slavery.
tossups.r: California became a state in 1850. For 10 points, name this event, which brought tens of thousands of “forty-niners” west.

tossups.p: The richest diggings of this event lay along a belt of gold-bearing rock in the Sierra Nevada foothills called the Mother Lode. Miners there swirled gravel in pans or rocked it in wooden cradles to wash away dirt and leave the heavy flakes behind.
tossups.r: Those miners were called “forty-niners.” For 10 points, name this event that began at Sutter’s Mill in 1848.

tossups.p: Late in this event, miners began blasting hillsides with high-pressure jets of water, a method called hydraulic mining that choked rivers downstream with mud. Earlier, miners had used shallow pans and long wooden troughs called sluices.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event that began when James Marshall found gold at Sutter’s Mill in 1848.

tossups.p: Henry Wells and William Fargo founded a company in 1852 to provide banking and to ship gold, money, and mail during this event. San Francisco grew from a village of about 1,000 people into a booming city during this event, and abandoned ships crowded its harbor.
tossups.r: That company was Wells Fargo. For 10 points, name this event that brought the “forty-niners” west after 1848.

tossups.p: Bret Harte’s story “The Luck of Roaring Camp” and Mark Twain’s “The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County” are set in mining camps that grew up during this event.
tossups.r: The song “Oh My Darling, Clementine” is about a “miner, forty-niner.” For 10 points, name this event that began in 1848.

tossups.p: A statue of one man stands over his grave at Coloma, pointing toward the spot where he made the discovery that started this event. That man’s employer, the Swiss immigrant John Sutter, lost his workers and most of his land to the fortune seekers who swarmed in.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this event, which began when James Marshall found gold at Sutter’s Mill in 1848.

tossups.p: An estimated 300,000 people came west during this event, many of them over the California Trail across the Sierra Nevada. The population boom allowed a new state to skip the territory stage and join the Union in 1850.
tossups.r: California’s motto, “Eureka” (“I have found it”), is said to refer to this event. For 10 points, name this event that brought the “forty-niners” west.

clues.t: Began when gold was found at Sutter’s Mill, a sawmill at Coloma, on January 24, 1848
Gold seekers who poured in during 1849 were called “forty-niners”; San Francisco’s NFL team is named for them
The carpenter James Marshall spotted the first flakes while building the sawmill
Helped California become the 31st state in 1850, as a free state under the Compromise of 1850
John Sutter, a Swiss immigrant, owned the mill; fortune seekers overran his land and he went broke
Merchant Sam Brannan waved a bottle of gold dust in the streets of San Francisco, then got rich selling supplies
President James K. Polk confirmed the discovery in his December 1848 message to Congress
Levi Strauss sold dry goods in San Francisco; in 1873 he and tailor Jacob Davis patented riveted denim pants (blue jeans)
Routes west: overland on the California Trail, by ship around Cape Horn, or across the Isthmus of Panama
Disease, starvation, and attacks by miners and state-backed militias cut California’s Native population from an estimated 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870
San Francisco boomed from a village of about 1,000 people into a city; abandoned ships crowded its harbor
Miners washed stream gravel in pans, rocking cradles, and wooden troughs called sluices
California’s motto, “Eureka” (“I have found it”), is said to refer to it; the state’s nickname is the Golden State
Chinese immigrants who came during it called California “Gold Mountain”
The Foreign Miners’ Tax (1850) charged non-citizens $20 a month, driving off many Mexican and Latin American miners; a later version hit the Chinese
Forty-niners called the hard trip and its disappointments “seeing the elephant”
Forty-niners were nicknamed “Argonauts,” after the heroes who sailed with Jason for the Golden Fleece
Forty-niners sang new words to Stephen Foster’s “Oh! Susanna” on the way west
The richest gold belt, in the Sierra Nevada foothills, was called the Mother Lode
Marshall found the flakes in the mill’s tailrace on the South Fork of the American River, nine days before the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
Later, hydraulic mining blasted hillsides with high-pressure water and choked rivers with mud
Henry Wells and William Fargo founded Wells Fargo (1852) for banking and for shipping gold, money, and mail
The folk song “Oh My Darling, Clementine” is about a “miner, forty-niner” and his daughter
Mining-camp stories: Bret Harte’s “The Luck of Roaring Camp” and Mark Twain’s “The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County”
The Land Act of 1851 made Californios (Spanish-speaking landowners) prove their land titles in court; many lost their ranches
An 1850 state law let settlers force Native people, including children, into unpaid labor; in 2019 Governor Gavin Newsom apologized, calling the violence a genocide
A statue of Marshall at Coloma stands over his grave, pointing toward the discovery spot; Sacramento grew up around Sutter’s Fort

trap.title: Which gold rush?
trap.body: Several gold rushes show up in quiz bowl. The California gold rush began at Sutter’s Mill in 1848 and peaked with the forty-niners in 1849. The Klondike Gold Rush (1896–1899) took place in Canada’s Yukon, reached through Alaska, and Georgia’s 1829 rush near Dahlonega helped push the Cherokee off their land. Charlie Chaplin’s famous 1925 film _The Gold Rush_ is set in the Klondike, not California.
trap.fix: Sutter’s Mill, James Marshall, Coloma, Sam Brannan, forty-niners, and Levi Strauss mean California. Skagway, Dawson City, and the Yukon mean the Klondike. Saying just “California” names the state, not the event, and a plain “gold rush” earns only a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: California gold rush (accept Gold Rush of 1849; prompt on gold rush; do not accept “California” alone)

topics.name: Chester A. Arthur
topics.kicker: 21st U.S. President · Signed the Pendleton Civil Service Act
topics.briefing: Chester Arthur spent years as a loyal member of Roscoe Conkling’s New York political machine, handing out jobs at the busy Port of New York. Then a disappointed office-seeker shot President James Garfield in 1881, and Arthur suddenly became the 21st president. To nearly everyone’s surprise, he backed reform and signed the Pendleton Act, which began filling some federal jobs through exams instead of political favors.
topics.answerHtml: Chester A. Arthur (or Chester Alan Arthur; do not accept “James Garfield”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Starting just before this man became president, a New York woman named Julia Sand wrote him a series of letters urging him to rise above machine politics, and he later paid her a surprise visit. Many reformers had expected the worst from this longtime ally of Roscoe Conkling.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who took office after the assassination of James Garfield.

tossups.p: During the 1880 campaign, opponents claimed that this man had secretly been born in Canada, which would have made him ineligible to be vice president. This man was actually born in Fairfield, Vermont, the son of a Baptist preacher from Ireland.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vice president who became the 21st president in 1881.

tossups.p: As a young lawyer, this man helped win a lawsuit for Elizabeth Jennings, a Black schoolteacher who had been forced off a New York City streetcar because of her race. During the Civil War, he served as quartermaster general of New York’s militia, supplying its troops.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York Republican who became president after James Garfield was killed.

tossups.p: Ulysses S. Grant named this man Collector of the Port of New York, a post that let him hand out hundreds of jobs at the busy Custom House. Rutherford B. Hayes removed him from that job in 1878 as part of a push for civil service reform.
tossups.r: This man later became vice president under James Garfield. For 10 points, name this Stalwart Republican who became the 21st president.

tossups.p: At the 1880 Republican convention, delegates chose this man as the running mate of a dark-horse nominee who won on the 36th ballot, hoping to please Stalwarts who had wanted Ulysses S. Grant to return. Roscoe Conkling urged this man to turn down the nomination, but he accepted.
tossups.r: That nominee was James Garfield. For 10 points, name this man who became president in 1881 after Garfield’s death.

tossups.p: After shooting a president at a Washington train station, Charles Guiteau [“gih-TOH”] shouted that he was “a Stalwart of the Stalwarts” and that this man would now be president. This man was sworn in at his New York City home in the middle of the night after that president died.
tossups.r: That president was James Garfield. For 10 points, name this vice president who succeeded Garfield and later signed the Pendleton Act.

tossups.p: This president signed a law that created the Civil Service Commission and made it illegal to fire certain federal workers for refusing to give money to a political party. Public anger over his predecessor’s assassination helped that law pass in 1883.
tossups.r: That law was the Pendleton Act. For 10 points, name this 21st president, who took office after James Garfield was killed.

tossups.p: This president vetoed a bill that would have banned Chinese laborers from immigrating for twenty years, saying it broke a treaty with China. He then signed a version that banned them for ten years, the first major U.S. law to keep out immigrants because of their nationality.
tossups.r: That 1882 law was the Chinese Exclusion Act. For 10 points, name this president who succeeded James Garfield.

tossups.p: This president vetoed the Rivers and Harbors Act of 1882 as wasteful spending, but Congress overrode his veto. He also signed the Tariff of 1883, which critics nicknamed the “Mongrel Tariff.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican president who served from 1881 to 1885, after the death of James Garfield.

tossups.p: This president is sometimes called the “Father of the Steel Navy” because Congress approved the first steel warships, the cruisers _Atlanta_, _Boston_, and _Chicago_ and the dispatch boat _Dolphin_, during his term. His secretary of the navy was William Chandler.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who took office after James Garfield died in 1881.

tossups.p: This president refused to move into the White House until it was redecorated, and he sold off about two dozen wagonloads of old furniture. Louis Comfort Tiffany then added a huge stained-glass screen to the mansion’s entrance hall.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this stylish president, nicknamed the “Gentleman Boss,” who succeeded James Garfield.

tossups.p: Soon after becoming president, this man learned he had Bright’s disease, a serious kidney illness, but he kept it secret. He made only a halfhearted try for his party’s nomination in 1884, which went to James G. Blaine, and he died two years later.
tossups.r: Earlier, he had signed the Pendleton Act. For 10 points, name this 21st president, who succeeded James Garfield.

tossups.p: During this man’s presidency, the International Meridian Conference in Washington chose Greenwich, England, as the starting point for measuring longitude. Near the end of his term, he dedicated the newly finished Washington Monument.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who succeeded James Garfield in 1881 and later signed the Pendleton Act.

tossups.p: This president’s Justice Department prosecuted the Star Route scandal, in which officials and contractors cheated the government on mail-delivery routes in the West. In 1883, he joined Governor Grover Cleveland at the opening of the Brooklyn Bridge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker, the 21st president of the United States.

tossups.p: Because his wife, Ellen, had died before he took office, this president’s sister Mary McElroy served as White House hostess. He served his entire term without a vice president, and shortly before his death he had most of his personal papers burned.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Stalwart Republican who became president after James Garfield was assassinated.

clues.t: 21st President of the United States (1881–1885), a Republican from New York
Vice president who took over when James Garfield died after being shot in 1881
Signed the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act (1883), which required exams for some federal jobs
Signed the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882), which banned Chinese laborers from immigrating for ten years
Ulysses S. Grant made him Collector of the Port of New York (1871), a job full of patronage at the Custom House
Rutherford B. Hayes removed him as Collector in 1878, in a push for civil service reform
A Stalwart Republican and ally of New York boss Roscoe Conkling, who opposed civil service reform
Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office-seeker, shot Garfield and shouted, “I am a Stalwart of the Stalwarts!”
Picked as Garfield’s running mate in 1880 to please the Stalwarts, after Garfield won the nomination on the 36th ballot
Sworn in at his New York City home in the middle of the night after Garfield died (September 1881)
Sometimes called the “Father of the Steel Navy”: the first steel warships (_Atlanta_, _Boston_, _Chicago_, and _Dolphin_) were approved in 1883
Had Louis Comfort Tiffany redecorate the White House, adding a stained-glass screen; sold about 24 wagonloads of old furniture
Nicknamed the “Gentleman Boss” for his fancy clothes and manners; wore bushy side-whiskers
Secretly had Bright’s disease, a kidney illness; barely tried for the 1884 nomination (won by James G. Blaine) and died in 1886
Born in Fairfield, Vermont (1829), son of an Irish-born Baptist preacher; opponents falsely claimed he was born in Canada
As a young lawyer, helped win the case of Elizabeth Jennings, a Black teacher forced off a New York City streetcar
Quartermaster general of New York’s militia during the Civil War
Julia Sand wrote him a series of letters urging him to rise above machine politics; he later visited her
Vetoed a first Chinese exclusion bill that would have lasted twenty years, saying it broke a treaty, then signed a ten-year version
Vetoed the Rivers and Harbors Act of 1882 as wasteful, but Congress overrode him
Signed the Tariff of 1883, nicknamed the “Mongrel Tariff”
His Justice Department prosecuted the Star Route scandal over cheating on Western mail-delivery contracts
Attended the opening of the Brooklyn Bridge (1883) with Governor Grover Cleveland
Dedicated the newly finished Washington Monument near the end of his term (1885)
The International Meridian Conference in Washington (1884) chose Greenwich, England, as the prime meridian
Had no vice president; his sister Mary McElroy was White House hostess because his wife, Ellen, had died in 1880
Had most of his personal papers burned shortly before he died

trap.title: Garfield’s successor, not Garfield
trap.body: Many clues in this man’s tossups are really about James Garfield: the 1880 election, the dark-horse convention, and Charles Guiteau’s attack. If a question asks for the president who was shot in 1881, the answer is Garfield; if it asks who took over and then signed the Pendleton Act, it is Arthur. Players also mix up the Gilded Age presidents between Grant and McKinley: Hayes (1877–1881), Garfield (1881), Arthur (1881–1885), Cleveland (1885–1889 and 1893–1897), and Benjamin Harrison (1889–1893).
trap.fix: Listen for what happened after September 1881: the Pendleton Act, the Chinese Exclusion Act, the Tiffany redecoration, and a background at the Port of New York all mean Arthur. Guiteau’s shout that “Arthur is president now” points to Arthur only when the question asks who took over.
trap.line: Real answer line: Chester Alan Arthur (do not accept or prompt on “James Garfield”)

topics.name: Colony of Virginia
topics.kicker: Founded at Jamestown in 1607 · England’s first permanent American colony
topics.briefing: The Colony of Virginia began in 1607, when the Virginia Company of London planted a settlement at Jamestown. Tobacco soon made it rich, and in 1619 it gained the first elected assembly in English America, the House of Burgesses, the same year the first recorded enslaved Africans arrived at Point Comfort. Virginia became a royal colony in 1624, and its leaders later helped launch the American Revolution.
topics.answerHtml: Colony of Virginia (or Virginia Colony; do not accept or prompt on “Jamestown”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Governor Alexander Spotswood of this colony sent the naval force that killed the pirate Blackbeard near Ocracoke Island in 1718. Spotswood also led an expedition across the Blue Ridge Mountains whose members were later called the Knights of the Golden Horseshoe.
tossups.r: Its capital by then was Williamsburg. For 10 points, name this English colony whose first permanent settlement was Jamestown.

tossups.p: This colony’s last royal governor, Lord Dunmore, issued a 1775 proclamation promising freedom to enslaved people who left Patriot owners to fight for the British. A year earlier, Dunmore had led a war against the Shawnee that was named for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony, home of George Washington and Thomas Jefferson, whose first settlement was Jamestown.

tossups.p: In the 1580s, Sir Walter Raleigh named the land later claimed by this colony in honor of Elizabeth I, the “Virgin Queen,” long before any lasting settlement was made there. Raleigh’s own failed colony stood on Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina.
tossups.r: John Smith and John Rolfe later lived in this colony. For 10 points, name this English colony founded at Jamestown in 1607.

tossups.p: On July 30, 1619, Governor George Yeardley opened this colony’s first General Assembly inside a church, making it the first elected lawmaking body in English America. Its elected members, two from each of the colony’s settlements, were called burgesses.
tossups.r: That assembly met at Jamestown. For 10 points, name this colony, where the House of Burgesses met.

tossups.p: In late August 1619, the privateer ship _White Lion_ landed at Point Comfort in this colony with “20 and odd” enslaved Africans who had been taken from a Portuguese slave ship. They were the first recorded Africans brought to English North America.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English colony whose House of Burgesses first met that same year at Jamestown.

tossups.p: Nathaniel Bacon led frontier settlers against this colony’s governor, William Berkeley, in a 1676 revolt, partly because Berkeley would not let them attack Native Americans. Bacon’s followers burned the capital, but the revolt fell apart after Bacon died of disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony whose first settlement, Jamestown, was burned in Bacon’s Rebellion.

tossups.p: Sir Thomas Dale enforced a harsh code called the “Laws Divine, Moral and Martial” in this colony, where settlers could be whipped for missing church. Earlier, the winter of 1609 to 1610 was so terrible that settlers called it the “Starving Time.”
tossups.r: Before that, John Smith had warned settlers that those who would not work would not eat. For 10 points, name this English colony whose first settlement was Jamestown.

tossups.p: The 1609 wreck of the _Sea Venture_ on Bermuda delayed help for this colony. In 1610, its new governor, Lord De La Warr, arrived just as hungry settlers were about to sail home, and a river was later named for him.
tossups.r: John Rolfe survived that shipwreck. For 10 points, name this English colony founded at Jamestown in 1607.

tossups.p: After Opechancanough’s [“oh-puh-CHAN-kuh-noh”] 1622 attack killed about a quarter of this colony’s English settlers, King James I took away the London Company’s charter. In 1624, this colony came under the king’s direct control, with governors chosen by the Crown.
tossups.r: John Smith had once led this colony’s first settlement. For 10 points, name this colony founded at Jamestown in 1607.

tossups.p: The Wren Building at this colony’s College of William & Mary, founded in 1693, is the oldest college building still in use in the United States. In 1699, this colony moved its capital to Middle Plantation, which was renamed Williamsburg.
tossups.r: Its first capital had been Jamestown. For 10 points, name this English colony.

tossups.p: This colony’s headright system gave 50 acres of land for each person whose voyage a settler paid for, so planters brought over thousands of indentured servants. Around 1620, men in this colony used its main crop to pay for the voyages of women who came over as brides.
tossups.r: That crop was tobacco, first grown for export by John Rolfe, the husband of Pocahontas. For 10 points, name this colony.

tossups.p: This colony’s nickname, “the Old Dominion,” supposedly honors its loyalty to the Crown during the English Civil War. George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and Patrick Henry all served in its legislature, which met at Williamsburg after 1699.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony, whose House of Burgesses first met at Jamestown in 1619.

tossups.p: King James I’s 1606 charter gave a joint-stock company based in London the right to start this colony, and a second company based in Plymouth, England, the right to settle farther north. The London group sent its first settlers in late 1606.
tossups.r: Those settlers founded Jamestown the next year. For 10 points, name this English colony.

tossups.p: When royal governors shut down this colony’s legislature in 1769 and again in 1774, many of its members met at the Raleigh Tavern in Williamsburg instead. In 1775, Patrick Henry urged this colony to arm itself, declaring, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colony, whose House of Burgesses was the first elected assembly in English America.

tossups.p: Christopher Newport commanded the three ships that carried this colony’s first settlers: the _Susan Constant_, the _Godspeed_, and the _Discovery_. Those settlers first landed at Cape Henry before choosing a site up a river that they named for their king.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English colony, where John Smith once led the settlement at Jamestown.

clues.t: Founded at Jamestown in 1607, the first permanent English settlement in North America
John Rolfe made tobacco its money crop (around 1612)
Its House of Burgesses (1619) was the first elected assembly in English America
John Smith led its first settlement for a time; Pocahontas, daughter of Powhatan, married John Rolfe
Started by a joint-stock company, the London Company, under King James I’s 1606 charter
August 1619: the _White Lion_ brought the first recorded enslaved Africans to Point Comfort
Became a royal colony in 1624, after the London Company lost its charter
Bacon’s Rebellion (1676): Nathaniel Bacon led frontier settlers against Governor William Berkeley and burned Jamestown
The capital moved from Jamestown to Middle Plantation, renamed Williamsburg, in 1699
The College of William & Mary was founded in 1693, second only to Harvard among colonial colleges
The “Starving Time” (winter of 1609–1610) nearly wiped out its first settlement
Opechancanough’s 1622 attack killed about a quarter of the English colonists
The headright system gave 50 acres for each person whose passage a settler paid, bringing over many indentured servants
Named for Queen Elizabeth I, the “Virgin Queen,” by Sir Walter Raleigh in the 1580s
Governor George Yeardley opened the first General Assembly in Jamestown’s church on July 30, 1619
Christopher Newport commanded the _Susan Constant_, _Godspeed_, and _Discovery_; the settlers first landed at Cape Henry
Sir Thomas Dale’s harsh “Laws Divine, Moral and Martial” (settlers could be whipped for missing church)
After the _Sea Venture_ wrecked on Bermuda (1609), Governor Lord De La Warr arrived in 1610 as settlers were leaving; the Delaware River is named for him
Berkeley would not let frontier settlers attack Native Americans; the revolt collapsed when Bacon died of disease (1676)
Around 1620, men paid for the voyages of brides from England with tobacco
Raleigh’s earlier colony on Roanoke Island (now North Carolina) failed; it became the “Lost Colony”
Nicknamed the “Old Dominion,” supposedly for its loyalty to the Crown during the English Civil War
Governor Alexander Spotswood sent the force that killed Blackbeard (1718) and led the Knights of the Golden Horseshoe over the Blue Ridge
Last royal governor Lord Dunmore promised freedom to enslaved people who fought for the British (1775); Dunmore’s War against the Shawnee (1774)
Patrick Henry: “Give me liberty, or give me death!” (1775); legislators met at the Raleigh Tavern when governors dissolved their assembly
George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, and Patrick Henry all served in its House of Burgesses

trap.title: Colony, not Jamestown
trap.body: Jamestown was only the first settlement in the Colony of Virginia. Real answer lines that want the colony say “do not accept or prompt on Jamestown,” so naming the town loses the tossup, even though many clues (John Smith, Pocahontas, the Starving Time, Bacon’s Rebellion) mention it. Don’t be fooled by Virginia Dare, either: the first English child born in the Americas was born in 1587 at Walter Raleigh’s “Lost Colony” of Roanoke, twenty years before Jamestown.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This settlement,” “this fort,” or “this town” means Jamestown; “this colony,” with clues stretching across decades (royal governors, Williamsburg, William & Mary, the 1619 assembly, Patrick Henry), means Virginia. Plymouth (1620, the Pilgrims) and Maryland (1634, the Calverts) are different colonies.
trap.line: Real answer line: Colony of Virginia (do not accept or prompt on “Jamestown”)

topics.name: Common Sense
topics.kicker: Thomas Paine’s 1776 pamphlet · Made the case for independence
topics.briefing: In January 1776, many colonists still hoped to make peace with King George III. Then an English immigrant named Thomas Paine published a short pamphlet in plain, punchy language, arguing that kings were a bad idea and that America should break away from Britain. Copies were reprinted across the colonies and read aloud in taverns, and six months later Congress declared independence.
topics.answerHtml: Common Sense (prompt on Thomas Paine; do not accept “The American Crisis” or “Rights of Man”)
reject: letters from a farmer in pennsylvania

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Loyalist James Chalmers answered this work with a pamphlet titled _Plain Truth_. This work’s author had arrived in Philadelphia just over a year before it appeared, carrying a letter of introduction from Benjamin Franklin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this January 1776 pamphlet in which Thomas Paine argued for American independence.

tossups.p: The Scottish-born printer Robert Bell published the first edition of this work, but its author quarreled with him over the profits and took an expanded edition, with an added appendix, to other printers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pamphlet, first published without its author’s name in 1776, in which Thomas Paine urged the colonies to break from Britain.

tossups.p: This work pointed to the Old Testament stories of Gideon, who refused to become king, and of the Israelites who demanded that the prophet Samuel give them a king. Its section “Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession” attacked the idea of passing a crown from parent to child.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this January 1776 pamphlet in which Thomas Paine urged the colonies to declare independence.

tossups.p: This work proposed a “Continental Charter” and a national congress whose president would come from a colony chosen by lot. It also argued that it was absurd for a continent to be ruled forever by an island.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pamphlet published in January 1776 by Thomas Paine, who argued for American independence.

tossups.p: John Adams disliked this work’s plan for a one-house legislature and wrote _Thoughts on Government_ partly in response. Even so, Adams admitted that its case for independence summed up arguments he had been making in Congress for months.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this best-selling pamphlet that Thomas Paine published in January 1776 to argue for independence.

tossups.p: This work mocked King George III as the “Royal Brute of Britain” and argued that any peace deal with Britain would only leave the quarrel for the next generation. Its author declared that “the cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1776 pamphlet by Thomas Paine that pushed the colonies toward independence.

tossups.p: This work opens by contrasting society with government, calling society “a blessing” but government, “even in its best state,” only “a necessary evil.” That first section also criticized Britain’s constitution, with its mix of king, lords, and commons. Later, it tells readers that “’Tis time to part.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this January 1776 pamphlet in which Thomas Paine called for independence from Britain.

tossups.p: This work’s author declared that “we have it in our power to begin the world over again” and argued that the colonies could build a navy of their own. Its fourth section discussed America’s present ability to defend itself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1776 pamphlet by Thomas Paine that called for independence from Britain.

tossups.p: In a letter written three weeks after this work appeared, George Washington praised its “sound doctrine and unanswerable reasoning.” Copies of this work were read aloud in taverns and passed from hand to hand across the colonies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pamphlet published in January 1776 by Thomas Paine.

tossups.p: Before writing this work, its author had worked in England as a corset maker and as a tax collector, and he had written a pamphlet asking Parliament to raise the pay of tax officers. He published this work without his name on it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pamphlet by Thomas Paine that argued for American independence in January 1776.

tossups.p: By some estimates, more than 100,000 copies of this work were sold in 1776, though historians disagree about the exact number. It was written in plain language so that ordinary farmers and workers could follow its arguments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pamphlet by Thomas Paine that argued for independence from Britain.

tossups.p: This work’s author later defended the French Revolution against Edmund Burke in _Rights of Man_ and promoted deism in _The Age of Reason_. During the Reign of Terror, he was jailed in Paris until James Monroe helped free him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1776 pamphlet, the first famous work of Thomas Paine.

tossups.p: Months after writing this work, its author began a series of essays that opens “These are the times that try men’s souls,” which George Washington had read to his troops shortly before the Battle of Trenton.
tossups.r: That series was _The American Crisis_. For 10 points, name this earlier 1776 pamphlet by Thomas Paine.

tossups.p: The physician Benjamin Rush encouraged a recent English immigrant to write this work and suggested its title. It first appeared without the author’s name, and some readers guessed it had been written by John Adams or Benjamin Franklin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pamphlet that Thomas Paine published in January 1776.

tossups.p: This work insisted that “Europe, and not England, is the parent country of America,” and it warned that ties to Britain kept dragging the colonies into Europe’s wars. Its author urged the colonies to declare independence months before Congress did.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pamphlet by Thomas Paine, published on January 10, 1776.

clues.t: Written by Thomas Paine, an English immigrant who had arrived in Philadelphia in 1774
Published in Philadelphia on January 10, 1776, half a year before the Declaration of Independence
Argued in plain language that the colonies should break away from Britain and declare independence
A short pamphlet and a huge best-seller (by some estimates, more than 100,000 copies in 1776), often read aloud in taverns
Attacked monarchy and hereditary succession, the idea of passing a crown from parent to child
Called King George III the “Royal Brute of Britain”
Said it was absurd for a continent to be ruled forever by an island
First published anonymously by the printer Robert Bell; some readers guessed John Adams or Benjamin Franklin wrote it
The physician Benjamin Rush encouraged Paine to write it and suggested the title
Society is “a blessing,” but government “even in its best state is but a necessary evil”
“The cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind”
George Washington praised its “sound doctrine and unanswerable reasoning” (January 1776)
Paine’s later series _The American Crisis_ (“These are the times that try men’s souls”) was read to Washington’s troops before Trenton
“We have it in our power to begin the world over again”; argued the colonies could build their own navy
Urged readers that “’Tis time to part” from Britain
Sections include “Of Monarchy and Hereditary Succession” and “Thoughts on the Present State of American Affairs”
Used Old Testament stories (Gideon refusing a crown; the Israelites demanding a king from Samuel) against monarchy
Proposed a “Continental Charter” and a congress whose president came from a colony chosen by lot
“Europe, and not England, is the parent country of America”; ties to Britain dragged the colonies into Europe’s wars
Paine quarreled with Robert Bell over profits and took an expanded edition, with an appendix, to other printers
The Loyalist James Chalmers answered it with the pamphlet _Plain Truth_
John Adams disliked its plan for a one-house legislature and wrote _Thoughts on Government_ partly in response
Paine came to Philadelphia in 1774 with a letter of introduction from Benjamin Franklin
In England, Paine had been a corset maker and an excise (tax) officer who wrote a pamphlet asking for better pay for tax officers
Paine later wrote _Rights of Man_ (defending the French Revolution against Edmund Burke) and _The Age of Reason_ (deism)
During the Reign of Terror, Paine was jailed in Paris until James Monroe helped free him (1794)

trap.title: The pamphlet, not the author
trap.body: The answer is the pamphlet, not the man who wrote it. Thomas Paine also wrote _The American Crisis_ (December 1776, “These are the times that try men’s souls”), _Rights of Man_ (1791), and _The Age of Reason_ (1790s), so clues about his later life can sneak into these tossups. Don’t confuse it with the Declaration of Independence, either: Paine’s pamphlet came out six months earlier and argued for independence; it did not declare it.
trap.fix: If you hear January 1776, Robert Bell, Benjamin Rush, the “Royal Brute of Britain,” or an island ruling a continent, say the title. On this site, “Thomas Paine” earns a prompt, but in a real match a moderator may simply rule the author wrong, so always name the pamphlet.
trap.line: Real answer line: Common Sense (do not accept “The American Crisis” or “Rights of Man”)
